claim: In humans, new-born infants can regenerate their heart during early life.
source: In humans, new-born infants can regenerate their heart during early life.
evidence: Supported by citation to Haubner et al., 2016 in the manuscript text

claim: The neonatal mouse heart exhibits a remarkable regenerative capacity after myocardial infarction (MI) up to 7 days after birth.
source: Unlike the adult mammalian heart, the neonatal mouse heart exhibits a remarkable regenerative capacity after myocardial infarction (MI) up to 7 days after birth (Aaboud et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Aaboud et al., 2018

claim: A similar regenerative capacity was shown in new-born humans.
source: A similar regenerative capacity was shown in new-born humans (Haubner et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Haubner et al., 2016

claim: The regenerative potential is linked to the epicardium, a mesothelial layer covering the outer surface of the heart.
source: This regenerative potential is linked to the epicardium, a mesothelial layer covering the outer surface of the heart.
evidence: Supported by inference from the context and subsequent citations

claim: During development, a subset of epicardial cells undergoes epithelial to mesenchyme transition (EMT), generating epicardium-derived cells (EPDCs) that contribute to coronary vessel formation and cardiomyocyte proliferation and compaction.
source: During development, a subset of epicardial cells undergoes epithelial to mesenchyme transition (EMT), generating epicardium-derived cells (EPDCs) that contribute to coronary vessel formation and cardiomyocyte proliferation and compaction (Simões and Riley, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Simões and Riley, 2018

claim: Wilms' tumour 1 (WT1) is instrumental in the regulation of EMT.
source: A number of transcription factors are expressed in the developing epicardium, including Wilms' tumour 1 (WT1), which is instrumental in the regulation of EMT.
evidence: Supported by inference from the context and subsequent citations

claim: Loss of WT1 impairs the ability of EPDCs to migrate into the underlying sub-epicardial region and mutant embryos die between E14.5 and E16.5 due to cardiovascular failure.
source: Loss of WT1 impairs the ability of EPDCs to migrate into the underlying sub-epicardial region and mutant embryos die between E14.5 and E16.5 due to cardiovascular failure (Martínez-Estrada et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Martínez-Estrada et al., 2010

claim: EPDC plasticity gradually decreases during embryogenesis and after birth, the epicardium becomes quiescent.
source: EPDC plasticity gradually decreases during embryogenesis and after birth, the epicardium becomes quiescent.
evidence: Supported by inference from the context and subsequent citations

claim: Embryonic genes, such as Wt1, are downregulated and EMT ceases after birth.
source: Embryonic genes, such as Wt1, are downregulated and EMT ceases (Zhou and Pu, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhou and Pu, 2011

claim: Following injury, the epicardium reactivates, resembling an embryonic-like state.
source: Following injury, the epicardium reactivates, resembling an embryonic-like state.
evidence: Supported by inference from the context and subsequent citations

claim: Epicardial cells re-express WT1 following injury.
source: Epicardial cells re-express WT1 (Wang et al., 2015), proliferate, undergo EMT, and differentiate into fibroblasts to stimulate tissue repair (Zhou et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2015

claim: Thymosin β4 (Tβ4) pre-treatment results in EPDC-mediated neovascularisation after injury.
source: Thymosin β4 (Tβ4) pre-treatment results in EPDC-mediated neovascularisation after injury (Smart et al., 2007a) and induces limited de novo cardiomyocyte formation by differentiation from a progenitor population of epicardial origin (Smart et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Smart et al., 2007a

claim: Hypoxia has been linked to tissue regeneration.
source: Hypoxia, or low oxygen levels, has been linked to tissue regeneration (Price et al., 2019), and hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs) play a central role in cellular responses to hypoxia (Kaelin and Ratcliffe, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Price et al., 2019

claim: Hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs) play a central role in cellular responses to hypoxia.
source: Hypoxia, or low oxygen levels, has been linked to tissue regeneration (Price et al., 2019), and hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs) play a central role in cellular responses to hypoxia (Kaelin and Ratcliffe, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kaelin and Ratcliffe, 2008

claim: HIFs are heterodimeric transcription factors, consisting of α and β subunits.
source: HIFs are heterodimeric transcription factors, consisting of α and β subunits (Dunwoodie, 2009), with the latter being constitutively expressed, whereas expression of the α subunit is oxygen-dependent (reviewed in Lee et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dunwoodie, 2009

claim: The β subunit of HIF is constitutively expressed, whereas expression of the α subunit is oxygen-dependent.
source: HIFs are heterodimeric transcription factors, consisting of α and β subunits (Dunwoodie, 2009), with the latter being constitutively expressed, whereas expression of the α subunit is oxygen-dependent (reviewed in Lee et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2019

claim: Under well-oxygenated conditions (i.e. normoxia), prolyl hydroxylase domain proteins (PHD1-3) hydroxylate specific conserved proline residues on the α subunit, tagging it for proteasomal degradation.
source: Under well-oxygenated conditions (i.e. normoxia), prolyl hydroxylase domain proteins (PHD1-3) hydroxylate specific conserved proline residues on the α subunit, tagging it for proteasomal degradation.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge and citation to Appelhoff et al., 2004

claim: When oxygen levels drop, PHD activity is inhibited, enabling the α subunit to translocate to the nucleus and bind to hypoxia response elements (HRE) regulating transcription of a plethora of target genes.
source: When oxygen levels drop, PHD activity is inhibited, enabling the α subunit to translocate to the nucleus and bind to hypoxia response elements (HRE) regulating transcription of a plethora of target genes (Appelhoff et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Appelhoff et al., 2004

claim: In humans, mice, and rats, there are three isoforms of the α subunit, but the best characterised are HIF-1α and HIF-2α activating distinct, although partially overlapping, sets of genes.
source: In humans, mice, and rats, there are three isoforms of the α subunit, but the best characterised are HIF-1α and HIF-2α activating distinct, although partially overlapping, sets of genes (Smythies et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Smythies et al., 2019

claim: Hypoxia and HIF activation are evident throughout the developing heart.
source: Hypoxia and HIF activation are evident throughout the developing heart (Dunwoodie, 2009) and disruption of oxygen sensing pathways during development results in a wide range of cardiac abnormalities (Romanowicz et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dunwoodie, 2009

claim: Disruption of oxygen sensing pathways during development results in a wide range of cardiac abnormalities.
source: Hypoxia and HIF activation are evident throughout the developing heart (Dunwoodie, 2009) and disruption of oxygen sensing pathways during development results in a wide range of cardiac abnormalities (Romanowicz et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Romanowicz et al., 2021

claim: WT1 expression is upregulated in the heart and kidneys of rats exposed to hypoxia.
source: Notably, WT1 expression is upregulated in the heart and kidneys of rats exposed to hypoxia and an HRE binding site for HIF-1α has been identified within the Wt1 promoter (Wagner et al., 2003) suggesting a link between hypoxia, HIF signalling, and epicardial activation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Wagner et al., 2003

claim: An HRE binding site for HIF-1α has been identified within the Wt1 promoter.
source: Notably, WT1 expression is upregulated in the heart and kidneys of rats exposed to hypoxia and an HRE binding site for HIF-1α has been identified within the Wt1 promoter (Wagner et al., 2003) suggesting a link between hypoxia, HIF signalling, and epicardial activation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Wagner et al., 2003

claim: Stabilising HIF-1α inhibits EPDC migration in avian embryos.
source: Studies have shown that stabilising HIF-1α inhibits EPDC migration in avian embryos (Tao et al., 2013) but promotes their differentiation into vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs; Tao et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tao et al., 2013

claim: Stabilising HIF-1α promotes EPDC differentiation into vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs).
source: Studies have shown that stabilising HIF-1α inhibits EPDC migration in avian embryos (Tao et al., 2013) but promotes their differentiation into vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs; Tao et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tao et al., 2018

claim: Endothelium-specific depletion of Egln1 and Eglin3 (encoding PHD2 and PHD3, respectively) promotes cardiomyocyte proliferation and prevents left ventricular failure in a model of MI.
source: Endothelium-specific depletion of Egln1 and Eglin3 (encoding PHD2 and PHD3, respectively) promotes cardiomyocyte proliferation and prevents left ventricular failure in a model of MI (Fan et al., 2019), and exposure to hypoxia following MI induces a regenerative response in adult mice by metabolic reprogramming of cardiomyocytes leading to cell cycle re-entry (Nakada et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fan et al., 2019

claim: Exposure to hypoxia following MI induces a regenerative response in adult mice by metabolic reprogramming of cardiomyocytes leading to cell cycle re-entry.
source: Endothelium-specific depletion of Egln1 and Eglin3 (encoding PHD2 and PHD3, respectively) promotes cardiomyocyte proliferation and prevents left ventricular failure in a model of MI (Fan et al., 2019), and exposure to hypoxia following MI induces a regenerative response in adult mice by metabolic reprogramming of cardiomyocytes leading to cell cycle re-entry (Nakada et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nakada et al., 2017

claim: The epicardium and subepicardial space are identified as hypoxic niches, housing a unique progenitor cell population.
source: The epicardium and subepicardial space are identified as hypoxic niches, housing a unique progenitor cell population (Kocabas et al., 2012; Hesse et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kocabas et al., 2012 and Hesse et al., 2021

claim: At E12.5, extensive regions of hypoxia were observed, mostly in areas of dense myocardium, such as the compact wall of the atrioventricular (AV) groove.
source: At E12.5, characterised by a well-established epicardial layer amidst highly trabeculated myocardium, we observed extensive regions of hypoxia, mostly in areas of dense myocardium, such as the compact wall of the atrioventricular (AV) groove (Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a using HP1 staining

claim: HP1 staining co-localised with the epicardial marker WT1 at E12.5.
source: Notably, HP1 staining co-localised with the epicardial marker WT1 (Figure 1a), and both HIF-1α (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a) and HIF-2α at the apex of the heart.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a

claim: Strong HIF-1α signals were noted at the base of the heart at E12.5.
source: Additionally, strong HIF-1α signals were noted at the base of the heart (Figure 1a), while HIF-2α expression extended into the myocardial compartment (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a

claim: HIF-2α expression extended into the myocardial compartment at E12.5.
source: Additionally, strong HIF-1α signals were noted at the base of the heart (Figure 1a), while HIF-2α expression extended into the myocardial compartment (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a

claim: By E14.5, extensive HP1 staining persisted in areas of thicker compact myocardium, such as the interventricular septum (IVS).
source: By E14.5, extensive HP1 staining persisted in areas of thicker compact myocardium, such as the interventricular septum (IVS; Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b

claim: Co-localisation with WT1 and HIF-1α was observed predominantly in the epicardium at E14.5, notably in the apex.
source: Co-localisation with WT1 and HIF-1α was observed predominantly in the epicardium, notably in the apex (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b), and base regions.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b

claim: Analysis of hearts at E16.5 and E18.5 revealed a progressive decrease in HP1 signal, becoming largely confined to WT1-expressing epicardial cells at later stages.
source: Analysis of hearts at E16.5 and E18.5 revealed a progressive decrease in HP1 signal, becoming largely confined to WT1-expressing epicardial cells at later stages (Figure 1c and d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c and d

claim: HIF-1α localisation was restricted in discrete regions of the outermost layer of the heart at E16.5 and E18.5.
source: Similarly, HIF-1α localisation was restricted in discrete regions of the outermost layer of the heart (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c, d), whereas HIF-2α expression transitioned from the epicardium (notably at the apex of the heart) to some sporadic expression in underlying cardiomyocytes by E18.5. (Figure 1—figure supplement 2c, d, Figure 1c and d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c, d

claim: WT1+ cells making up the epicardial layer of the developing heart become hypoxic from mid-gestation onwards, preferentially expressing HIF-1α.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that WT1+ cells making up the epicardial layer of the developing heart become hypoxic from mid-gestation onwards, preferentially expressing HIF-1α, whereas HIF-2α expression predominantly occurs within the forming myocardium.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data presented in Figure 1 and supplements

claim: HIF-2α expression predominantly occurs within the forming myocardium.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that WT1+ cells making up the epicardial layer of the developing heart become hypoxic from mid-gestation onwards, preferentially expressing HIF-1α, whereas HIF-2α expression predominantly occurs within the forming myocardium.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data presented in Figure 1 and supplements

claim: Epicardial-specific deletion of Hif1α resulted in a marked reduction in the number of WT1+ cells in mutant (KO) hearts as compared to littermate controls (CTR) at E16.5.
source: Immunostaining for WT1 and the epicardial marker podoplanin (PDPN) revealed a marked reduction in the number of WT1+ cells in Wt1CreERT2/+;Hif1afl/fl mutant (KO) hearts as compared to littermate controls (CTR; Figure 2a and b), affecting both the epicardial layer (Figure 2c; CTR: 0.72±0.11; KO: 0.32±0.010; p=0.0268) and the myocardium (Figure 2d; CTR: 3.96±1.01; KO: 0.98±0.25; p=0.0461).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a-d with statistical analysis

claim: Deletion of Hif1a did not affect HIF-2α expression in WT1+ cells.
source: Notably, deletion of Hif1a did not affect HIF-2α expression in WT1+ cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a

claim: No significant alterations were observed in myocardial compaction in Hif1α mutants.
source: No significant alterations were observed in myocardial compaction (Figure 2e), myocardial trabeculation as assessed by fractal analysis (Figure 2f), or the proliferation rate of WT1+ cells between mutants and controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c, d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2e

claim: Mutant hearts exhibited significantly impaired coronary vasculature, as evidenced by decreased total vessel length, number of junctions and vessel end points.
source: Mutant hearts exhibited significantly impaired coronary vasculature, as evidenced by decreased total vessel length (microns; Figure 2h, CTR: 129229±5509; KO: 81073±10915; p=0.0170), number of junctions (Figure 2i, Mean ± SEM; CTR: 2505±63.74; KO: 1457±282.1; P=0.0223) and vessel end points (Figure 2j, Mean ± SEM; CTR: 3422±249.5; KO: 2429±218.6; p=0.0402).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2h-j with statistical analysis

claim: Tamoxifen-treated epicardial explants from Wt1CreERT2/+;Hif1afl/fl embryos showed a reduced HIF-1α expression.
source: Epicardial explants from Wt1CreERT2/+;Hif1afl/fl embryos treated with tamoxifen showed a reduced HIF-1α expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 2b; CTR: 0.99±0.16; KO: 0.46±0.12; p=0.0397) without affecting HIF-2α levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 2c; CTR: 2505±63.74; KO: 1457±282.1; p=0.223).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2b with statistical analysis

claim: Tamoxifen-treated epicardial explants from Wt1CreERT2/+;Hif1afl/fl hearts revealed an increased epithelial and reduced mesenchymal phenotype.
source: Tamoxifen-treated epicardial explants from Wt1CreERT2/+;Hif1afl/fl hearts revealed an increased epithelial and reduced mesenchymal phenotype. This was evident by reduced stress fibre formation (Figure 2k), reduced alpha-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA) staining (Figure 2l), and altered sub-cellular localisation of the EMT marker and structural component of cell-cell adhesion complexes zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1) (Figure 2m) compared to controls.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2k-m

claim: Explants derived from Wt1CreERT2/+;Hif1αfl/fl embryos exhibited decreased WT1 expression, indicating impaired epicardial EMT.
source: Consistent with our in vivo findings, explants derived from Wt1CreERT2/+;Hif1αfl/fl embryos exhibited decreased WT1 expression, indicating impaired epicardial EMT (Figure 2n and o; CTR: 725.7±86.93; KO: 490.9±37.65; p=0.0479).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2n and o with statistical analysis

claim: ChIP-seq analysis confirmed direct HIF binding within intron 3 of the Wt1 gene.
source: ChIP-seq analysis confirmed direct HIF binding within intron 3 of the Wt1 gene (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), consistent with previous findings (Wagner et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and citation to Wagner et al., 2003

claim: Rosa26+/CreERT2; Egln1fl/fl derived explants (KO) exhibited a significant induction of HIF-1α and HIF-2α expression as compared to controls (CTR) upon tamoxifen treatment.
source: Upon tamoxifen treatment, Rosa26+/CreERT2; Egln1fl/fl derived explants (KO) exhibited a significant induction of HIF-1α and HIF-2α expression as compared to controls (CTR; Figure 3—figure supplement 1a–c; HIF-1α; CTR: 0.26±0.13; KO: 0.86±0.09; p=0.0061; HIF-2α; CTR: 0.37±0.01; KO: 1.12±0.15; p=0.0027).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a-c with statistical analysis

claim: Visualization of stress fibres via α-SMA staining revealed augmented mesenchymal morphology in the Egln1 mutant-derived explants.
source: Subsequent visualisation of stress fibres via α-SMA staining revealed augmented mesenchymal morphology in the mutant-derived explants (Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a

claim: WT1 nuclear fluorescence was significantly increased in Egln1-KO explants as compared to controls.
source: Consistent with this, WT1 nuclear fluorescence was significantly increased in KO explants as compared to controls (CTR; Figure 3b and c; CTR: 158.7±48.34; KO: 330.5±27.26; p=0.0364).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b and c with statistical analysis

claim: Expression levels of the EMT transcription factor snail family transcriptional repressor 2 (Snai2) gene were increased in Egln1-KO explants relative to CTR.
source: In addition, expression levels of the EMT transcription factor snail family transcriptional repressor 2 (Snai2) gene were increased in Egln1-KO explants relative to CTR (Figure 3d; CTR: 1±0.025; KO: 1.166±0.036; p=0.0464).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3d with statistical analysis

claim: Immunostaining for HIF-1α and HIF-2α confirmed the stabilisation of HIF signalling upon PHD inhibitor treatment.
source: Immunostaining for HIF-1α and HIF-2α confirmed the stabilisation of HIF signalling upon PHD inhibitor treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d–g).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1d-g

claim: Staining with phalloidin and α-SMA showed an enhanced mesenchymal morphology with increased stress fibres in inhibitor-treated explants, suggestive of EMT induction.
source: Staining with phalloidin (Figure 3e) and α-SMA (Figure 3f) showed an enhanced mesenchymal morphology with increased stress fibres in inhibitor-treated explants, suggestive of EMT induction.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3e and f

claim: Immunostaining demonstrated a significant increase in WT1 expression in Molidustat-treated explants as compared to control.
source: Furthermore, immunostaining demonstrated a significant increase in WT1 expression in treated explants as compared to control (Figure 3g and h; CTR: 1039±134.9; Mol: 2500±503.7; P=0.03).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3g and h with statistical analysis

claim: The PHD inhibitor enhanced the motility of cultured mouse embryonic ventricular epicardial cells (MEC.1 cell line) compared to control-treated cells.
source: Likewise, the PHD inhibitor enhanced the motility of cultured mouse embryonic ventricular epicardial cells (MEC.1 cell line) (Li et al., 2011) compared to control-treated cells (Figure 3i and j; CTR: 436869±9359; Mol: 372482±20880; p=0.0477), as assessed by scratch assays.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3i and j with statistical analysis

claim: Gene Ontology (GO) analysis for biological processes showed an enrichment of hypoxia-related pathways in P1 compared to P7 hearts.
source: Gene Ontology (GO) analysis for biological processes showed an enrichment of hypoxia-related pathways in P1 compared to P7 hearts (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a), particularly in the epicardial cell population (Figure 4c).
evidence: Supported by single cell RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a and Figure 4c

claim: Hypoxia-related pathways were enriched in P7 hearts compared to P1 hearts in the fibroblast cluster.
source: In contrast, hypoxia-related pathways were enriched in P7 hearts compared to P1 hearts in the fibroblast cluster (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b–d), suggesting a role for hypoxia post-injury, specifically in the fibrotic response leading to scarring.
evidence: Supported by single cell RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b-d

claim: Expression of well-known HIF-induced genes such as Vegfa and pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase 3 (Pdk3) was increased in P1-derived epicardial cells.
source: Accordingly, expression of well-known HIF-induced genes such as Vegfa and pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase 3 (Pdk3) was increased in P1-derived epicardial cells (Figure 4d).
evidence: Supported by single cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4d

claim: The expression of Egln1, encoding for the main suppressor of HIF signalling, was enriched in P7 cells.
source: Conversely, the expression of Egln1, encoding for the main suppressor of HIF signalling, was enriched in P7 cells (Figure 4e).
evidence: Supported by single cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4e

claim: A time-course analysis of mRNA levels using ventricle lysates and immunostaining revealed a marked upregulation of Egln1 cardiac levels from P7 to adulthood.
source: These findings were further confirmed by a time-course analysis of mRNA levels using ventricle lysates and immunostaining which revealed a marked upregulation of Egln1 cardiac levels from P7 to adulthood (Figure 4f, Figure 4—figure supplement 2a, b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4f and Figure 4—figure supplement 2a, b

claim: The increase in Egln1 levels coincided with a reduction in WT1 expression in P7 versus P1 hearts.
source: Notably, this increase in Egln1 levels coincided with a reduction in WT1 expression in P7 versus P1 hearts (Figure 4g).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4g

claim: Immunostaining analysis of the endothelial marker CD31 and α-SMA did not reveal a significant difference in the number of vessels between Egln1fl/fl (CTR) and Wt1CreERT2; Egln1fl/fl (KO) hearts at 21 dpi.
source: Immunostaining analysis of the endothelial marker CD31 and α-SMA did not reveal a significant difference in the number of vessels between Egln1fl/fl (CTR) and Wt1CreERT2; Egln1fl/fl (KO) hearts (Figure 5b and c, CTR 0.0030±0.0004, KO 0.0034±0.0002, p=0.45), suggesting that activation of HIF signalling in WT1-expressing cells does not affect the neovascularisation response.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5b and c with statistical analysis

claim: Cine-MRI analysis at 3 weeks post-MI showed a substantial increase in the ejection fraction (EF) and decrease in the end-diastolic volume (EDV) in Wt1CreERT2; Egln1fl/fl (KO) animals compared to controls.
source: To investigate whether epicardial activation of HIF signalling improved heart function following MI, we performed cine-MRI analysis at 3 weeks post-MI. We observed a substantial increase in the ejection fraction (EF) and decrease in the end-diastolic volume (EDV) in KO animals compared to controls (Figure 5d–f; EF: CTR 43.21±6.25, KO 64.30±6.82, p<0.05. EDV; CTR 54.19±3.50, KO 33.72±2.67; p<0.05).
evidence: Supported by MRI data shown in Figure 5d-f with statistical analysis

claim: Histological analysis by Masson's trichrome staining revealed a significant reduction of the fibrotic scar in Wt1CreERT2; Egln1fl/fl (KO) animals as compared to controls.
source: Furthermore, histological analysis by Masson's trichrome staining revealed a significant reduction of the fibrotic scar in KO animals as compared to controls (Figure 5g and h, CTR 15.44±1.088, KO 10.34±1.374, p=0.027) without changes in the size of cardiomyocytes, as assessed by wheat germ agglutinin staining (WGA; Figure 5i and j, CTR 167.6±3.27, KO 179.3±8.68, p=0.32).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 5g and h with statistical analysis

claim: Treatment with PHD inhibitor effectively stabilised HIF-1α and HIF-2α in hearts collected at 9 days post-MI (9dpi).
source: Treatment with PHD inhibitor effectively stabilised HIF-1α and HIF-2α, as observed by immunostaining (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a, b) in hearts collected at 9 days post-MI (9dpi).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a, b

claim: Pharmacological approach revealed a significant increase in epicardial WT1 expression in both the infarct and remote zones in Molidustat-treated hearts compared to controls.
source: Moreover, this pharmacological approach revealed a significant increase in epicardial WT1 expression in both the infarct and remote zones (Figure 6b) in Molidustat-treated hearts (MI T) compared to controls (CTR) (Figure 6c and d, infarct zone: MI CTR 0.34±0.08, MI T 0.50±0.06, remote zone: CTR 0.075±0.02, MI T 0.25±0.05, p<0.05).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6b-d with statistical analysis

claim: An increase in WT1 expression in the myocardium was observed in the PHD-inhibitor treated group and was more pronounced proximal to the infarct region.
source: Similarly, an increase in WT1 expression in the myocardium was observed in the PHD-inhibitor treated group and was more pronounced proximal to the infarct region (Figure 6e and f, infarct zone: CTR 5.02±1.34, MI T 7.09±1.86, p=<0.05; remote zone: CTR 13.88±4.96, MI T 18.61±6.18; p<0.05).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6e and f with statistical analysis

claim: An extensive co-localisation of WT1 and EMCN was observed within the myocardial compartment at 9 dpi, supporting an endothelial identity for these cells.
source: We observed an extensive co-localisation of WT1 and EMCN within the myocardial compartment at 9 dpi (Figure 6—figure supplement 1c), supporting an endothelial identity for these cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1c

claim: An assessment of the proliferation of WT1+ cells and cardiomyocytes revealed no significant differences between control and Molidustat-treated animals.
source: Furthermore, an assessment of the proliferation of WT1+ cells and cardiomyocytes revealed no significant differences between control and Molidustat-treated animals (Figure 6—figure supplement 1d, e, g).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1d, e, g

claim: Co-immunostaining and quantification of CD31 and α-SMA revealed no difference in the number of vessels between controls and the Molidustat treatment group at 21 dpi.
source: To analyse the long-term histological effects of HIF-stabilisation after MI, we collected hearts at 21 dpi. Co-immunostaining and quantification of CD31 and α-SMA revealed no difference in the number of vessels between controls and the treatment group (Figure 6g and h).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6g and h

claim: Cine-MRI analysis showed a marked reduction in left ventricular systolic function following MI in the vehicle-treated group (MI CTR) as compared to uninjured hearts (Sh).
source: Cine-MRI analysis showed a marked reduction in left ventricular systolic function following MI in the vehicle-treated group (MI CTR) as compared to uninjured hearts (Sh) and, more importantly, a significant improvement in systolic function in the PHD inhibitor treated groups (MI T).
evidence: Supported by MRI data shown in Figure 6i and j

claim: EF and EDV were significantly improved in the Molidustat-treated groups.
source: EF and EDV were significantly improved in the drug-treated groups (Figure 6i and j; EF: Sh 78.10±3.22, MI CTR 67.70±4.31, MI T 77.61±1.76, p<0.05; EDV: Sh 27.53±3.10, MI CTR 36.11±2.49 MI T 26.44±0.93; p<0.05).
evidence: Supported by MRI data shown in Figure 6i and j with statistical analysis

claim: Histological analysis by Masson's trichrome staining revealed the presence of a fibrotic scar in drug-treated animals, albeit this was reduced relative to controls.
source: Histological analysis by Masson's trichrome staining revealed the presence of a fibrotic scar in drug-treated animals, albeit this was reduced relative to controls (Figure 6k and l) and the at-risk myocardium was comparatively thicker with minimal dilatation or thinning of the left ventricle.
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 6k and l

claim: The thickened myocardium was not due to an effect on cardiomyocyte hypertrophy, as determined by WGA staining.
source: The thickened myocardium was not due to an effect on cardiomyocyte hypertrophy, as determined by WGA staining (Figure 6—figure supplement 1f–h) nor an effect on cardiomyocyte proliferation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1e, g) suggesting potential cardio-protection and improved preservation of survived heart muscle.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1f-h

claim: At E12.5, hypoxia was mainly observed in areas of compact myocardium, most significantly in the atrioventricular (AV) groove, close to where the coronary plexus first develops.
source: At E12.5, hypoxia was mainly observed in areas of compact myocardium, most significantly in the atrioventricular (AV) groove, close to where the coronary plexus first develops (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to Chen et al., 2014
